RC1.title: Measurement and its discontents
RC1.text: Every measurement regime begins as an act of humility and ends as an act of governance. When a hospital first begins to track waiting times, the figure is merely a window onto its operations; once administrators tie funding to that figure, it becomes a lever, and levers invite handling. Wards learn to reclassify patients as 'admitted' the moment they cross the threshold, even if they linger in corridors for hours. The metric improves; the experience of waiting does not. The economist Charles Goodhart's observation that a measure ceases to be a good measure once it becomes a target is often quoted as though it were a lament about human dishonesty. This is too generous to the measurers and too harsh on the measured. Those who game a target are usually responding rationally to an incentive designed by someone who mistook a proxy for the thing itself. The deeper failure is conceptual: a proxy is valuable precisely because it is cheap to observe relative to the quality it stands for, and that cheapness is also what makes it cheap to counterfeit. Remedies exist, but none is free. Rotating metrics frustrate manipulation but deprive institutions of the stable benchmarks they need for learning. Pairing quantitative measures with qualitative audits restores context but reintroduces discretion, the very thing metrics were meant to discipline. Perhaps the sober conclusion is that measurement should be treated less as a mirror than as a conversation: one in which every number is provisional, and the more consequential the number, the more suspicious one ought to be of it.

RC2.title: The tyranny of the timetable
RC2.text: Before the railways, time in Britain was a local affair. Bristol kept its clocks about ten minutes behind London, and nobody was troubled, because nobody moved fast enough for the discrepancy to matter. The railway timetable changed this not by making people more punctual but by making lateness legible: a train either left at the printed hour or it did not, and a passenger who arrived by the town clock found the platform empty. Standardisation, in this telling, was a gift of technology to a world awaiting it. Yet historians have lately complained that such accounts smuggle in an assumption of inevitability. Many towns resisted 'railway time' for decades; Bristol's Corn Exchange famously displayed two minute hands, one for each regime, and some merchants elsewhere insisted that the sun, not the company, was the proper authority over their afternoons. What eventually secured uniformity was less the superiority of the new system than the accumulated cost of dissent. Each institution that adopted the standard (post office, court, telegraph) raised the penalty for the next that did not, until local time survived only as a sentimental affectation. The lesson is not that the railways were innocent. It is that a convention triumphs when opting out becomes expensive, whether or not opting in was ever the better choice, and that the 'obviousness' we later attach to a standard is often an artefact of its victory rather than its cause.

RC3.title: In praise of the empty hour
RC3.text: Boredom is generally treated as a malfunction of modern life, a vacuum that devices were invented to fill. But the psychologist's older view, that boredom is a signal rather than a state, deserves revival. A bored mind is not an idle one; it is one that has detected a mismatch between its capacities and its surroundings and is pressing for adjustment. In that sense boredom resembles hunger: unpleasant by design, and valuable because the discomfort compels action. The trouble begins when the remedy is too instant. A person who answers every flicker of restlessness with a screen never lets the signal complete its work, and so never discovers what the restlessness was pointing towards, whether a neglected ambition, a dissatisfaction with a job, or merely the need for rest. Critics might object that this romanticises tedium, since the boredom of a factory line or a waiting room is hardly generative. The objection has force, but it conflates boredom that is imposed with boredom that is endured by choice. Experiments suggest that people who are permitted to remain with an unstimulating task for a while later produce more original solutions to open-ended problems than those who were diverted. The effect is modest and not uniformly replicated, and one should resist the temptation to prescribe boredom as a tonic. Still, a culture that regards every empty interval as a problem to be solved may be quietly eliminating the conditions under which some of its best ideas arise.

CA1.title: Conversation: 'Partners' or 'dependants'? (The Policy Hour)
CA1.text:
CONVERSATION ANALYSIS: Read the following transcript and choose the answer that is closest to each of the questions that are based on the transcript.

Meera Kapoor (Host, The Policy Hour): Dr. Rao, platform companies call their drivers 'partners'. You prefer the word 'dependants'. Why?

Dr. Anil Rao (labour economist): Because partnership implies bargaining power, and these workers have almost none. A driver cannot set the fare, cannot see the destination before accepting, and can be deactivated by an algorithm without appeal. Flexibility is real, but it is flexibility to log in, not flexibility over terms.

Meera Kapoor: The platforms say workers value the freedom.

Dr. Anil Rao: Many do, and I don't dismiss it. But surveys of freedom are usually taken from people who have other options. For someone with a car loan to service, a 'free' schedule often means working twelve hours because any single hour pays too little. The freedom is sometimes the mechanism of the squeeze.

Meera Kapoor: So regulation?

Dr. Anil Rao: Not necessarily employment status for all. I would begin with transparency: show the worker how the fare was computed and let them contest a deactivation. You cannot negotiate what you cannot see.

questions.question: The minister's assurances were so ________ that even her allies began to suspect the policy had been designed more to soothe than to solve.
options: categorical
incendiary
peremptory
anodyne
questions.explanation: 'Anodyne' means deliberately inoffensive and bland, intended to avoid controversy or upset. The clue is 'designed more to soothe than to solve': assurances meant to calm rather than commit. 'Categorical' (absolute) and 'peremptory' (imperious) suggest firmness, which would not make allies suspect a lack of substance; 'incendiary' (inflammatory) is the opposite of soothing.

questions.question: Far from being a ________ discovery, the vaccine was the culmination of decades of patient, incremental work by hundreds of researchers.
options: seminal
inconsequential
serendipitous
sporadic
questions.explanation: 'Far from being...' signals contrast with 'decades of patient, incremental work'. The opposite of planned, cumulative effort is a lucky accident, i.e. 'serendipitous'. 'Seminal' (groundbreaking) does not contrast with long effort; 'specious' (superficially plausible but false) and 'sporadic' (occasional) do not fit the logic.

questions.question: Critics dismissed the novel as ________, its elaborate plot concealing the fact that it had nothing new to say.
options: prosaic
indecipherable
pedantic
meretricious
questions.explanation: 'Meretricious' means showily attractive but without real value, exactly what an elaborate plot hiding emptiness is. 'Prosaic' (dull, ordinary) conflicts with 'elaborate'; 'laconic' (using few words) conflicts with an elaborate plot; 'pedantic' (overly concerned with detail/rules) does not capture the idea of false glitter.

questions.question: Many hail the new tax as a game changer, but it is hardly a ________; the fiscal deficit will persist unless spending is also brought under control.
options: dark horse
magic bullet
sitting duck
wild goose chase
questions.explanation: A 'magic bullet' (like 'silver bullet') is a single, simple solution to a complex problem. The 'but... unless spending is controlled' structure says the tax alone will not fix the deficit. 'Dark horse' (an unexpected winner), 'sitting duck' (an easy target) and 'wild goose chase' (a futile pursuit) do not fit the meaning.

questions.question: The diplomat's ________ manner masked a ________ resolve; negotiators who mistook his courtesy for weakness soon found him ________ on every substantive point.
options: brusque; feeble; flexible
urbane; steely; immovable
affable; vacillating; intransigent
gauche; adamant; obliging
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts a polished, courteous exterior ('urbane') with a hard inner resolve ('steely'), so negotiators found him 'immovable'. In (B) 'brusque' contradicts 'courtesy'. In (C) 'vacillating' (wavering) contradicts 'resolve'. In (D) 'gauche' (awkward) contradicts courtesy and 'obliging' contradicts 'soon found him...' on every point.

questions.question: A growing ________ of evidence suggests the firm's accounts were ________, yet regulators, wary of ________ allegations, have proceeded cautiously.
options: dearth; impeccable; credible
body; falsified; unproven
paucity; embellished; malicious
plethora; audited; scrupulous
questions.explanation: A growing 'body' of evidence suggesting 'falsified' accounts explains why regulators are wary of 'unsubstantiated' allegations and so move cautiously. 'Dearth/paucity' cannot be 'growing' in a way that supports suspicion; 'impeccable' and 'audited' do not suggest wrongdoing; 'credible' and 'scrupulous' allegations would not make regulators cautious.

questions.question: Her ________ prose, free of ornament, was a deliberate ________ to the ________ style then fashionable among her contemporaries.
options: ornate; rebuke; florid
turgid; tribute; austere
lucid; homage; ornate
spare; rebuke; florid
questions.explanation: 'Free of ornament' means 'spare'. A deliberate challenge to the then-fashionable style is a 'rebuke', and that style must be the opposite of spare, i.e. 'florid'. (B) 'ornate prose' contradicts 'free of ornament'; (C) 'turgid' (bloated) contradicts it as well; (D) 'homage to an ornate style' contradicts 'deliberate' contrast.

questions.question: The scientist's reluctance to publish was not mere ________; she had learnt that premature claims, once ________, are almost impossible to ________.
options: diffidence; retracted; amplify
caution; suppressed; revive
vanity; endorsed; verify
timidity; circulated; retract
questions.explanation: Her reluctance had a rational basis: once a premature claim is 'circulated' it can hardly be 'retracted'. 'Not mere timidity' sets up a contrast with a considered reason. (A) repeats the idea of shyness and 'amplify' makes no sense; (C) 'caution' is the very reason, so 'not mere caution' contradicts the logic; (D) 'vanity... endorsed... verify' is incoherent.

questions.question: Although the village appeared ________ to outsiders, its residents were ________ by a long-standing feud that had ________ every attempt at reconciliation.
options: tranquil; riven; thwarted
prosperous; united; facilitated
squalid; sustained; precipitated
remote; galvanised; hastened
questions.explanation: 'Although' sets up a contrast between a calm appearance ('tranquil') and inner division ('riven' = split apart), with the feud 'thwarting' reconciliation. The other options either do not contrast (squalid, remote) or reverse the meaning (united, facilitated, hastened).

questions.question: Neither the manager nor the employees <u>was aware</u> that the policy had changed.
options: has been aware
is aware
were aware
was being aware
questions.explanation: With 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. The nearer subject is the plural 'employees', so the verb must be plural: 'were aware'. The tense also matches 'had changed' (past). The other options are singular or change the tense unnecessarily.

questions.question: Hardly had the speaker begun her address <u>than</u> the lights went out.
options: then
when
while
than that
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' (like 'scarcely') is paired with 'when', not 'than'. 'No sooner... than' is the parallel construction. 'Then' and 'while' do not complete the correlative pair.

questions.question: Each of the proposals submitted by the contractors <u>were</u> rejected for failing to meet the safety norms.
options: was
have been
are
being
questions.explanation: 'Each' is a singular pronoun and takes a singular verb, regardless of the plural noun 'contractors' in the intervening phrase. 'Was rejected' is the correct form and agrees with the past context.

questions.question: The chairman's speech, <u>replete of</u> statistics but devoid of insight, left investors unimpressed.
options: replete with
replete in
repeating with
replete on
questions.explanation: 'Replete' takes the preposition 'with' (replete with = abundantly filled with). 'Replete of', 'in' and 'on' are all unidiomatic; 'repeating with' changes the word and makes no sense.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The minister's remarks were widely interpreted as an oblique criticism of the central bank's recent policy.
The novelist's early work is often eclipsed by her more celebrated and commercially successful later novels.
Her meticulous planning ensured the expedition ran effusively from start to finish.
The treaty was finally ratified after many months of acrimonious debate in both houses.
questions.explanation: 'Effusively' means in an unrestrained, gushing manner and cannot describe how an expedition runs; the intended word is 'smoothly'. In the other sentences 'oblique' (indirect), 'eclipsed' (overshadowed) and 'acrimonious' (bitter) are all used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The defendant's alibi was so flimsy that it collapsed under cursory questioning.
The sudden downpour exacerbated the villagers' hopes of a good harvest.
The museum's collection is notable for its eclectic range, spanning Roman coins to modern posters.
The diplomat's apology, though gracious, did little to mitigate the damage already done.
questions.explanation: 'Exacerbate' means to make something bad worse, so it cannot apply to 'hopes'; the intended word is 'dashed' or 'dampened'. 'Cursory' (hasty), 'eclectic' (drawn from diverse sources) and 'mitigate' (lessen) are used correctly in the rest.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The company's expansion was predicated on the assumption that consumer demand would keep growing.
The brothers, once inseparable, grew inured to each other after the inheritance quarrel.
The witness's testimony was corroborated by two entirely independent sources.
She was chastened by the criticism and promptly redoubled her efforts.
questions.explanation: 'Inured' means accustomed to something unpleasant; it does not describe the relationship between estranged brothers. The correct word is 'estranged' or 'alienated'. 'Predicated on' (based on), 'corroborated' (confirmed) and 'chastened' (subdued by criticism) are correct.

questions.question: Across Gujarat and Rajasthan, stepwells were built not merely to store water but to be inhabited. ____________________. Their cool, shaded chambers offered travellers respite from the heat, and their carved pillars hosted festivals and gatherings. By the time colonial administrators began piping water to towns, the stepwell's social role had already outlived its practical one.
options: They were, in effect, public squares that happened to hold water.
Most stepwells were eventually abandoned because they were expensive and difficult to maintain over time.
The colonial government was deeply impressed by the engineering sophistication of these structures.
Water scarcity in western India has since been aggravated by the spread of intensive modern agriculture.
questions.explanation: The blank must bridge 'built to be inhabited' and the details that follow (shaded chambers, festivals). Only the first option generalises that social function. The others introduce abandonment, colonial admiration and agriculture, none of which is developed in the next sentences.

questions.question: Open-source software is frequently described as free, but the word hides a subtle bargain. ____________________. Companies that build products on volunteer-maintained code enjoy its benefits without bearing its upkeep, and the volunteers, often unpaid, are left to absorb the burden. The arrangement works only as long as goodwill outlasts fatigue.
options: Many programmers contribute to open-source projects in order to build their professional reputations and networks.
Proprietary software, by contrast, is generally better documented and considerably more secure than most community tools.
Governments in several countries have begun mandating the use of open-source tools in public offices and agencies.
Its price is zero; its cost is simply borne by someone else.
questions.explanation: The following sentences explain who bears the hidden cost (volunteers) while companies benefit. The correct option states the 'bargain' directly (zero price, cost transferred). The others are true-sounding but shift to motivation, security and government policy.

questions.question: The Hindi word jugaad is often rendered in English as 'frugal innovation', a phrase that flatters it. ____________________. A truck engine bolted to a cart or a phone charger fixed with tape is clever, but it is also a quiet comment on the absence of better options. To celebrate the ingenuity without asking why it was needed is to admire the patch and ignore the hole.
options: Jugaad has attracted growing interest from management scholars in Europe and America, who study it as a model of low-cost product design.
Improvisation born of scarcity is as much a symptom of neglect as a sign of creativity.
Indian engineers are often reluctant to adopt formal design methodologies because these are seen as expensive and unnecessarily bureaucratic.
Foreign companies have frequently failed in the Indian market because of their reliance on technologies that ordinary consumers cannot afford.
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that 'frugal innovation' flatters jugaad because it hides the neglect behind it ('admire the patch and ignore the hole'). Only the correct option previews that two-sided claim. The others praise or discuss jugaad from the management, engineering or market angle, which the paragraph does not develop.

questions.question: Dr. Rao prefers the word 'dependants' over 'partners' because he believes that gig workers
options: lack real bargaining power over the terms of work
are paid less than workers in traditional employment
are unwilling to accept flexible schedules from platforms
cannot afford to own the vehicles that they drive
questions.explanation: Rao says partnership 'implies bargaining power, and these workers have almost none'; they cannot set fares, see destinations or contest deactivation. The other options (low pay relative to employees, unwillingness to accept flexibility, inability to own vehicles) are not claimed. In fact he mentions a car loan, so ownership is not the issue.

questions.question: According to Dr. Rao, the flexibility offered by platforms is best described as
options: a genuine benefit that outweighs any lack of bargaining power
an illusion, since drivers are forced to work fixed shifts
freedom to start work but not to shape the conditions
an advantage available only to workers who own their own cars
questions.explanation: Rao says the flexibility is 'real' but is 'flexibility to log in, not flexibility over terms'. He does not call it an illusion or claim fixed shifts exist, nor does he say it outweighs the problems or is limited to car owners.

questions.question: Dr. Rao questions surveys showing that workers value freedom because the respondents
options: are selected by the platforms themselves and therefore tend to give systematically biased answers
often have alternatives, so results may miss the financially squeezed
generally want regular employment instead of flexible work arrangements of any kind
do not understand how fares are calculated by the platform's algorithm
questions.explanation: Rao says such surveys 'are usually taken from people who have other options', whereas a worker servicing a loan may feel compelled to work long hours. He does not allege platform-chosen samples, a general preference for employment, or ignorance about fares.

questions.question: The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

sentences.1: This process, known as bleaching, is not immediately fatal, but a coral that stays bleached for long will starve.
sentences.2: Corals owe their colour and most of their energy to symbiotic algae living in their tissues.
sentences.3: Recovery is possible only if the heat subsides quickly enough for the algae to recolonise.
sentences.4: When water temperatures rise even slightly above seasonal norms, the corals expel these algae, leaving their white skeletons visible.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 introduces corals and their algae (the topic). Sentence 4 explains what happens when water warms: the algae are expelled. Sentence 1 begins 'This process, known as bleaching', which refers back to the expulsion in 4. Sentence 3 discusses recovery, which only makes sense after bleaching has been described and its severity noted. Order: 2-4-1-3.

questions.question: The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

sentences.1: Yet the Indian mathematicians who first treated it as a number in its own right, rather than a mere gap, did something conceptually radical.
sentences.2: For centuries, zero existed only as a placeholder, a way of telling 305 from 35 in Babylonian practice.
sentences.3: Brahmagupta, in the seventh century, laid down rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with it.
sentences.4: Even he stumbled over division by zero, a problem that would not be settled satisfactorily for another millennium.
sentences.5: The placeholder, in other words, had no arithmetic life of its own.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 opens with zero as a placeholder. Sentence 5 ('in other words') restates that point: the placeholder had no arithmetic life. Sentence 1 ('Yet...') introduces the contrast: Indian mathematicians treated zero as a number. Sentence 3 gives the concrete example (Brahmagupta's rules). Sentence 4 ('Even he...') follows naturally, noting his limitation. Order: 2-5-1-3-4.

questions.question: The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

sentences.1: The appeal is obvious: a system that screens thousands of résumés in seconds promises both speed and impartiality.
sentences.2: A model trained to replicate past success will therefore quietly reproduce past bias, now with the veneer of objectivity.
sentences.3: Companies increasingly deploy algorithms to filter job applicants before any human reads their applications.
sentences.4: But such systems learn from historical hiring decisions, and those decisions carry the prejudices of the people who made them.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 introduces the topic (companies using algorithms). Sentence 1 ('The appeal') explains why. Sentence 4 ('But...') presents the problem: historical data carries bias. Sentence 2 ('therefore') draws the conclusion from 4. Order: 3-1-4-2.

questions.question: The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

sentences.1: The reality was messier, since early printed books imitated manuscripts so closely that buyers sometimes could not tell them apart.
sentences.2: Scribes, far from vanishing, found new employment as illuminators, proofreaders and correctors for the printers.
sentences.3: When Gutenberg's press arrived in the mid-fifteenth century, it is often said to have killed the manuscript trade overnight.
sentences.4: Hence the revolution was one of habit before it was one of technology.
sentences.5: Their craft was displaced only gradually, as printers realised that books need not look handwritten to sell.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states the popular claim. Sentence 1 ('The reality was messier') challenges it. Sentence 2 introduces scribes, giving a concrete case of continued employment. Sentence 5 ('Their craft...') refers back to the scribes and their gradual displacement. Sentence 4 ('Hence...') concludes the argument. Order: 3-1-2-5-4.

questions.question: The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Each sentence is labelled with a number. Decide on the most logical order and enter only the sequence of numbers in the space provided.

sentences.1: This replay appears to help consolidate fragile new memories into durable ones.
sentences.2: Recordings of neural activity have overturned this assumption.
sentences.3: Sleep was long regarded as a passive interval during which the brain simply rested.
sentences.4: During deep sleep, patterns of firing that occurred during the day are replayed at accelerated speed.

questions.explanation: Sentence 3 gives the old view. Sentence 2 ('this assumption') overturns it. Sentence 4 describes what the recordings revealed: replay during deep sleep. Sentence 1 ('This replay') explains its function. Order: 3-2-4-1.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: Institutions that depend on quantitative metrics are inherently dishonest and should replace numbers with human judgement wherever the stakes are significant
Linking rewards to a proxy corrupts it, so measures should be held provisionally and sceptically
Goodhart's observation, widely treated as a complaint about dishonesty, in fact applies only to hospitals and similar public bodies
Rotating metrics and qualitative audits together offer a complete solution to the problem of manipulated measurement in organisations
questions.explanation: The passage shows that once a measure becomes a target, people respond to the incentive and the proxy loses value (a design flaw, not just dishonesty), and it ends by recommending that every number be treated as provisional. (B) contradicts the author's view that dishonesty is not the main issue; (C) restricts the claim to hospitals, though they are only an example; (D) overstates: the remedies are said to be costly and none is 'free'.

questions.question: The hospital example is used primarily to show that
options: a reported figure can improve while the experience it represents stays the same
administrators deliberately deceive regulators in order to secure additional funding for their wards
waiting times are an unusually unreliable metric compared with other indicators of hospital performance
patients left in corridors receive worse clinical care than those formally admitted to a ward
questions.explanation: The line 'The metric improves; the experience of waiting does not' states the purpose directly. The example illustrates a general point about proxies. The passage does not claim deception for funding, special unreliability of waiting times, or differences in clinical care.

questions.question: The author's remark that Goodhart's observation is 'too generous to the measurers and too harsh on the measured' suggests that the author believes
options: people who game targets should be excused because dishonesty is a natural human trait
measurers deliberately create flawed targets so that the measured can be blamed for failures
Goodhart himself intended his observation to be read as a defence of institutions rather than a criticism
those who design the incentives bear most of the responsibility for the distortion
questions.explanation: The next sentence says gamers are 'responding rationally to an incentive designed by someone who mistook a proxy for the thing itself'. Hence the fault lies with the designers (measurers), who are treated too generously by the dishonesty reading. The passage never says dishonesty is natural, that designers act deliberately, or what Goodhart intended.

questions.question: All of the following can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT:
options: Qualitative audits make quantitative metrics unnecessary in institutions
A proxy's ease of observation is both a source of its usefulness and of its vulnerability to manipulation
Rotating metrics can reduce manipulation but make long-term comparison and learning harder
Pairing numbers with qualitative review restores context at the cost of greater discretion
questions.explanation: (B), (C) and (D) are directly supported: 'cheap to observe... cheap to counterfeit'; rotating metrics lose 'stable benchmarks'; qualitative audits restore context but 'reintroduce discretion'. Nothing suggests audits make metrics unnecessary; they are offered as a partner to them, so (A) is the exception.

questions.question: The tone of the concluding sentence of the passage is best described as
options: bitterly cynical about the possibility of any reliable measurement
wistfully nostalgic for an era before institutions relied on numbers
enthusiastically optimistic about reforming measurement practices
measured and cautiously sceptical
questions.explanation: The author calls the conclusion 'sober' and advises suspicion of consequential numbers without rejecting measurement altogether. That is measured scepticism, not bitter cynicism, nostalgia or optimism.

questions.question: The author describes measurement as 'less a mirror than a conversation' in order to suggest that
options: numbers should be questioned and revised rather than accepted as neutral reflections
institutions should publish their metrics so that the public can debate each figure openly
measurement is inherently subjective, and therefore no number can ever be considered accurate
statisticians ought to consult those being measured before choosing which indicators to report
questions.explanation: A mirror passively reflects reality; a conversation involves exchange, challenge and revision. The author adds that 'every number is provisional'. The other options import ideas not in the passage: public debate, complete subjectivity, or consulting the measured.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: argue that railways alone made people more punctual in nineteenth-century Britain
defend local timekeeping traditions against standardisation imposed by railway companies and public institutions
question the view that standard time spread simply because it was inevitable or superior
demonstrate that every technological change is resisted by communities until the cost of resistance rises
questions.explanation: After presenting the 'gift of technology' account, the author says historians complain it assumes inevitability, then argues that uniformity was secured by the rising cost of dissent. (B) is explicitly denied ('not by making people more punctual'); (C) defends something the author does not defend; (D) over-generalises from time to all technology.

questions.question: In the passage, the phrase 'making lateness legible' most nearly means
options: teaching passengers to read printed timetables with accuracy
making deviation from a schedule visible and measurable
punishing passengers who failed to arrive at the platform on time
ensuring that every station clock displayed exactly the same hour
questions.explanation: Before the railways, discrepancies did not matter because there was no fixed standard. A printed timetable made it clear whether a train was on time or not, so lateness became observable. The other options misread 'legible' as literacy, punishment or clock uniformity.

questions.question: Why does the author mention the clock at Bristol's Corn Exchange with two minute hands?
options: To prove that Bristol was the last city in Britain to give up its own local time in favour of the railways' schedule
To illustrate that clockmakers resisted standardisation more fiercely than merchants did in the nineteenth century
To suggest that local time was in fact more accurate than railway time, as many residents then believed
To show the two systems coexisted for a time rather than one replacing the other at once
questions.explanation: The two hands are offered as evidence that towns 'resisted railway time for decades' and that both regimes were displayed together. The passage does not claim Bristol was the last city, compare clockmakers with merchants, or say local time was more accurate.

questions.question: Which of the following best reflects the author's view of why uniform time eventually prevailed?
options: Its greater accuracy over solar time convinced even the most sceptical merchants
Parliament passed legislation that forced towns to abandon their local clocks
The telegraph made it technically impossible to keep separate local times
Each adopter made refusal costlier for the institutions yet to adopt
questions.explanation: The passage says uniformity was secured by 'the accumulated cost of dissent': each institution that adopted the standard 'raised the penalty for the next that did not'. Superior accuracy is rejected explicitly ('less the superiority of the new system'), and legislation and technical impossibility are never mentioned.

questions.question: The author's final sentence implies that the apparent 'obviousness' of a standard is
options: a retrospective impression produced by its success
clear proof that the standard was objectively the best available option
a deliberate illusion fostered by those who profited from its adoption
something that fades gradually as local alternatives are forgotten
questions.explanation: The author calls obviousness 'an artefact of its victory rather than its cause': we find the standard obvious because it won, not the other way round. This is a hindsight effect. The passage neither equates obviousness with quality nor suggests deliberate manipulation or fading.

questions.question: As used in the passage, 'sentimental affectation' suggests that local time, in its last phase, was
options: kept up for show and fondness, not because it served any practical purpose
practised mainly by elderly citizens who could not understand the railway timetable
defended by merchants as a matter of principle rather than for sentiment
tolerated by courts and post offices as a harmless legal alternative
questions.explanation: An 'affectation' is a show put on, and 'sentimental' indicates fondness. Together they mean local time was retained for nostalgia and display after institutions had abandoned it. The other options bring in elderly citizens, principled merchants or legal tolerance, none of which is stated.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Boredom is a harmful malfunction of modern life that technology has fortunately learned to eliminate from daily experience
Creativity can be reliably produced by deliberately exposing people to long periods of monotonous work
Boredom works as a signal worth heeding, and instant distraction may cost us its benefits
The psychologists' older view of boredom has now been conclusively confirmed by laboratory experiments
questions.explanation: The passage revives the view of boredom as a signal, argues that instant remedies prevent the signal from working, and ends by warning that eliminating empty intervals may hurt idea generation. (B) is the view the author is arguing against; (C) is rejected ('resist the temptation to prescribe boredom'); (D) overstates the evidence, which is 'modest and not uniformly replicated'.

questions.question: The comparison between boredom and hunger primarily serves to show that boredom
options: can be satisfied completely by supplying the appropriate form of stimulation
arises from a physical deficiency and so cannot be controlled by the mind
is unpleasant by design, as the discomfort spurs corrective action
should be avoided whenever possible since it is a symptom of mental ill-health
questions.explanation: The passage says the resemblance lies in being 'unpleasant by design, and valuable because the discomfort compels action'. The analogy is about function and motivation, not about satisfying it with stimulation, physical origin or mental ill-health.

questions.question: The author answers the objection about factory-line boredom by
options: arguing that repetitive work is in fact more generative than creative work in most cases
conceding that boredom is harmful in every setting and beneficial in none whatsoever
distinguishing boredom that is imposed from boredom that is endured by choice
claiming that factory workers are far less affected by boredom than office workers are
questions.explanation: The author says the objection 'has force' but 'conflates boredom that is imposed with boredom that is endured by choice'. The reply is a distinction, not a denial of the objection, and the other options attribute claims the author never makes.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the experimental findings cited is best described as
options: dismissive, since they have not been replicated in factory settings or other real workplaces
convinced that they establish boredom as a reliable cure for a lack of originality
interested but cautious about how much weight they can bear
indifferent, as the passage rests chiefly on the psychologist's older view of boredom
questions.explanation: The author reports the finding but immediately notes the effect is 'modest and not uniformly replicated' and warns against prescribing boredom as a tonic. This is cautious interest. The passage does not mention factory-setting replications and does not call the findings conclusive.

questions.question: With which of the following would the author most likely disagree?
options: Instant remedies for restlessness may prevent people from understanding its cause
Boredom can carry information about a mismatch between a person and their surroundings
Prolonged boredom in monotonous work is a dependable source of creative ideas
It would be unwise to prescribe boredom as a general tonic for creativity
questions.explanation: The author concedes that the boredom of a factory line or a waiting room 'is hardly generative' and warns against prescribing it as a tonic. (B), (C) and (D) restate points the author makes in the passage.

questions.question: The final sentence suggests that a culture which treats every empty interval as a problem
options: has deliberately chosen efficiency over creativity as a collective priority
will inevitably produce fewer original ideas than cultures which accept boredom
is mistaken in thinking that unoccupied time can ever be put to productive use
may unintentionally be removing the conditions in which valuable ideas emerge
questions.explanation: The key words are 'may be quietly eliminating the conditions...': a hedged claim about an unintended side effect. (B) ascribes deliberate choice; (C) uses 'inevitably', which overstates the hedged claim; (D) uses 'ever', which is also too absolute since the author accepts that imposed tedium is unproductive in some settings.
